issues.legal_issue: A challenge to an order rejecting a plaint must be pursued through the available first appeal, and a writ petition challenging that order may be dismissed while leaving the appellate remedy open.
material_facts: The trial court rejected the plaint.
The plaintiff challenged the rejection by filing a writ petition rather than a first appeal.
The order rejecting the plaint is treated as a decree, from which a first appeal is available.
issues.conclusion: The writ petition was liable to be dismissed because the order rejecting the plaint was appealable as a decree; the plaintiff remained at liberty to pursue the remedy available under the Code of Civil Procedure.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure defines a decree to include rejection of a plaint. Under Section 96, a decree is appealable. Order 7 Rule 13 provides that rejection of a plaint does not by itself preclude presentation of a fresh plaint on the same cause of action. The Court therefore upheld dismissal of the writ petition on the ground that a first appeal was available, while leaving the plaintiff free to pursue the remedy in law.

predicates.writ_challenges_plaint_rejection: The plaintiff challenged an order rejecting a plaint by bringing a writ petition.
predicates.trial_court_rejected_plaint: The trial court rejected the plaintiff's plaint.
predicates.first_appeal_available: A first appeal was available against the order rejecting the plaint.

issues.definition: When a plaintiff uses a writ petition to challenge a trial court's rejection of a plaint and a first appeal is available, the writ petition is dismissed while the plaintiff may pursue that alternative remedy.

issues.legal_issue: A court that rejects a plaint because the suit appears from its statements to be barred by law cannot grant the plaintiff time to amend the plaint after rejection.
material_facts: The trial court allowed an application to reject the plaint because the suit appeared to be barred by law.
After allowing the application, the trial court directed the plaintiff to seek proper relief and pay the required court fee within a fixed time.
The statutory provision allowing additional time for correcting valuation or supplying stamp paper concerns those specific grounds for rejection, not rejection because the suit appears barred by law.
issues.conclusion: The direction permitting amendment after rejection of the plaint was not in accordance with law.
issues.legal_principle: Order 7 Rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure requires rejection where the suit appears from the statements in the plaint to be barred by law. The proviso to that rule concerns time fixed for correcting valuation or supplying requisite stamp paper in cases under clauses (b) and (c), and does not apply to rejection under clause (d). The Court relied on this distinction in holding that the trial court's further direction was not in accordance with law.

predicates.plaint_rejected_as_barred_by_law: The court rejected the plaint because the suit appeared from its statements to be barred by law.
predicates.court_granted_post_rejection_amendment_t: After rejecting the plaint, the court gave the plaintiff time to amend it and pay the required court fee.

issues.definition: When a court rejects a plaint because the suit appears barred by law and then gives the plaintiff time to amend it, the post-rejection amendment direction is not permitted.
